L31: ###### Abstract
L32: 
L33: Let $m$ be a fixed positive integer. It is well-known that a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,...,n\}$ may have one, many, or no $m$th roots. In this article we provide an explicit expression and a generating function for the number of $m$th roots of $\sigma$. Let $p_{m}(n)$ be the probability that a random $n$-permutation has an $m$th root. We also include a proof that $p_{m}(jq)=p_{m}(jq+1)=\cdots=p_{m}(jq+(q-1))$, $j=0,1,...$, when $m$ is a power of prime number $q$.
L34: ## 1 Introduction and main results
L35: Let $S_{n}$ be the group of all permutations of the finite set $[n]=\{1,...,n\}$. Let $m$ be a fixed positive integer. We say that $\sigma\in S_{n}$ has an $m$th root or that $\sigma$ is an $m$th power if there exists a permutation $\tau$ with $\tau^{m}=\sigma$.
L36: For fixed $m$, not all permutations have an $m$th root ([cite15†14 ], Theorem 4.8.2), however, Glebsky and Rivera [cite16†6 ] have proved that for sufficiently large $n$, any permutation has an “almost” $m$th root (in the sense of the Hamming distance [cite17†5 ]). Now, if we know that a permutation $\sigma$ has at least one $m$th root, how many $m$th roots can $\sigma$ have? Some results about this problem can be found in the paper of Pavlov [cite18†9 ] who gives an explicit expression for this quantity.
L37: Also, in the article of Annin, Jansen and Smith [cite19†1 ], appeared a classification of the elements in $S_{n}$ and $A_{n}$ that has $m$th roots, and they propose some problems related with the roots of permutations. In particular, our work is about some questions in Problem 1 of Annin et al.
L38: The main results of this paper are an explicit expression for the number of $m$th roots of any $n$-permutation $\sigma$ (Theorem cite20†1 ) and a generating function for this number (Theorem cite21†2 ). To obtain our expression we define some sets of non-negative integers that seems interesting in their own right (see Section cite7†2 ). These sets allows us to obtain a more simple expression that the expression of Pavlov [cite18†9 ]. Even more, a nice generating function is obtained in terms of one of these sets.
L39: Another classical problem consist in estimating the number of permutations in $S_{n}$ that admit an $m$th root. Turán [cite22†13 ] gave an upper bound when $m$ is a prime number and Blum [cite23†2 ] gave an asymptotic formula for the case $m=2$. Bóna, McLennan and White [cite24†4 ] proved that the probability that a random permutation of length $n$ has a $m$th root, $m$ prime, is monotonically non-increasing in $n$.
L40: See also the work of Pouyanne [cite25†11 ] for an asymptotic study for any positive integer $m$ and the work of B. Bollobás and B. Pittel [cite26†3 ] who continued the work of Pouyanne and studied the limiting distribution of the root degree of a permutation. This problem can be easily reformulated as the problem about the probability that a $n$-permutation chosen uniformly at random has an $m$th root ($p_{m}(n)$).
L41: For this problem, we give a proof of the fact that when $m$ is a power of a prime $q$, for all $j\geq 0$, $p_{m}(jq)=p_{m}(jq+1)=\cdots=p_{m}(jq+(q-1))$. For the case $m$ a prime, see the paper of Bóna, et al. [cite24†4 ] that includes a combinatorial proof of the equivalent equalities. Also recommended is the paper of A. Maróti [cite27†8 ] and the bibliography therein for related results about the proportion of $\ell$-regular elements in the symmetric group $S_{n}$.

L180: ## 3 Roots of permutations
L181: 
L182: Let $\sigma$ be an $n$-permutation. Let $m$ be a fixed positive integer. There may or may not exist a permutation $\tau$ that satisfies $\tau^{m}=\sigma$. If such $\tau$ exists, is called an $m$th root of $\sigma$. The following theorem gives a characterization of the $n$-permutations that has $m$th roots.
L183: ###### Theorem 3.
L184: 
L185: [cite15†14 , Theorem 4.8.2] Let $m$ be a positive integer. A permutation $\sigma$ has an $m$th root if and only if for every $\ell=1,2,...$ the number of $\ell$-cycles that $\sigma$ has is divisible by $((\ell,m))$.
L186: This theorem gives us information about the cycle structure of permutations that admits $m$th roots. But, if we know that a permutation has $m$th roots, we need a procedure to get all of its roots (see, for example [cite41†7 , §3.3]). The first important observation is that we can construct any $m$th root $\tau$ of $\sigma$ if we worked with cycles of $\sigma$ with different lengths separately.
L187: Indeed, if $\tau$ is an $m$th root of $\sigma$, with $\tau=C_{1}\cdots C_{s}$ its disjoint cycle factorization, then $\sigma=\tau^{m}=C_{1}^{m}\cdots C_{s}^{m}$, where $C_{i}^{m}$ consist in $\gcd(|C_{i}|,m)$ cycles of length $|C_{i}|/\gcd(|C_{i}|,m)$ each. Let $\sigma_{\ell}$ be the part of $\sigma$, that consist in the product of all cycles $D_{i}$ of length $\ell$ in $\sigma$ ($a_{\ell}\neq 0$, where $a_{\ell}$ is the number of cycles of length $\ell$ in $\sigma$).
L188: So, we can see permutation $\sigma$ as a product of parts $\sigma_{\ell}$, where every part $\sigma_{\ell}$ consist in all the cycles of length $\ell$ in the disjoint cycle factorization of $\sigma$. Let $\tau_{\ell}$ be the part of $\tau$ whose $m$th power produces the part $\sigma_{\ell}$
L189:  | $$\tau_{\ell}^{m}=\sigma_{\ell}=\prod_{\mid D_{i}\mid=\ell}D_{i}.$$  |
L190: And we can found $\tau_{\ell}$, and therefore $\tau$, working with $\sigma_{\ell}$ independently. This is for every length $\ell\neq 0$ in cycles of $\sigma$. Now, we need to found the admissible lengths, $|C_{i}|$, of cycles in $\tau_{\ell}$. We know that for any cycle $C_{i}$ in $\tau_{\ell}$, $|C_{i}|=\ell\gcd(|C_{i}|,m)$, and we write $g=\gcd(|C_{i}|,m)$. We need to found $g\leq a_{\ell}$, in such a way that $g=\gcd(g\ell,m)$.

Thus, any $g$ cycles of $\sigma_{\ell}$, $D_{i_{1}},\cdots,D_{i_{g}}$, can be combined in a suitable way (see, for example, proof of Theorem 3 in [cite19†1 ] or proof of Theorem 4.8.2 in [cite15†14 ]) into one $g\ell$-cycle $C_{i}$ for $\tau_{\ell}$ with $C_{i}^{m}=D_{i_{1}}\cdots D_{i_{g}}$.

L182: Let $\sigma$ be an $n$-permutation. Let $m$ be a fixed positive integer. There may or may not exist a permutation $\tau$ that satisfies $\tau^{m}=\sigma$. L185: [cite15†14 , Theorem 4.8.2] Let $m$ be a positive integer. A permutation $\sigma$ has an $m$th root if and only if for every $\ell=1,2,...$ the number of $\ell$-cycles that $\sigma$ has is divisible by $((\ell,m))$.

L61: ## 2. Preliminaries
L62: 
L63: This section provides some background material and minor results. We start by fixing some basic notation and reviewing the structural description of the functional graph of the power map on cyclic groups. Then we show how to extend this structural description for abelian groups. At the end of this section we provide some general results on the functional graph of the power map over arbitrary finite groups.
L64: Along the paper we use the letters $G,H$ to denote finite groups and $C$ to denote cyclic groups. For a positive integer $m$, $\mathcal{C}_{m}$ denotes the cyclic group of order $m$. We use multiplicative notation for the operation of these groups unless otherwise specified. The ring of integers modulo $d$ is denoted by $\mathbb{Z}_{d}$ and their multiplicative group of units is denoted by $\mathbb{Z}_{d}^{*}$.
L65: The Euler totient function is denoted by $\varphi(d)$ and the (multiplicative) order of $t\in\mathbb{Z}_{d}^{*}$ is denoted by $\ord_{d}(t)$. For a group $G$, the centralizer of $S\subseteq G$ is denoted by $C_{G}(S)$ and the center of $G$ is denoted by $Z(G)=C_{G}(G)$.
L66: ### 2.1. Basics on functional graphs
L67: We use the same terminology as in [cite29†14 ] and [cite36†17 ]. It is a well known fact that the connected components of functional graphs are composed of a cycle and each vertex of this cycle is the root of a tree (the direction of the edges is from leaves to the root). Several interesting classes of functions over finite fields or finite structures studied in the literature present certain regularity that is reflected in some symmetry conditions on their functional graphs.
L68: We denote by $\operatorname{Cyc}(m,T)$ a directed graph composed by an $m$-cycle (i.e. a cycle of length $m$) where every node in this cycle is the root of a tree isomorphic to $T$.
L69: When every connected component of a functional graph $\mathcal{G}(f/S)$ is of this form we say that this functional graph is regular, in this case there are integers $m_{1},\ldots,m_{k}$ and rooted trees $T_{1},\ldots,T_{k}$ such that $\mathcal{G}(f/S)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{k}\operatorname{Cyc}(m_{i},T_{i})$, where the circled plus symbol denotes a disjoint union of graphs. When the rooted tree $T$ has a unique vertex we write $T=\bullet$.
L70: The $m$-cycle $\operatorname{Cyc}(m,\bullet)$ is denoted by $\operatorname{Cyc}(m)$ and the rooted tree $T$ with a loop in the root $\operatorname{Cyc}(1,T)$ is denoted by $\{T\}$. The notation $G=k\times H$ means that $G=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{k}H_{i}$ with each $H_{i}$ isomorphic to the graph $H$. A forest is a disjoint union of rooted trees.
L71: Given a forest $G=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{k}T_{i}$, we denote by $\langle G\rangle$ the rooted tree with $k$ children where these children are roots of trees isomorphic to $T_{1},\ldots,T_{k}$. We consider the empty graph $\emptyset$ with the property that $\langle\emptyset\rangle=\bullet$. Given rooted trees $T_{1}=\langle G_{1}\rangle,\cdots,T_{k}=\langle G_{k}\rangle$ where each $G_{i}$ is a forest we define $\sum_{i=1}^{k}T_{i}:=\langle\bigoplus_{i=1}^{k}G_{i}\rangle$ (i.e.
L72: the sum of rooted trees is a new rooted tree which is obtained by identifying all the roots). For a tree $T=\langle G\rangle$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$ we denote $k\cdot T=\langle k\times G\rangle$ (note that $k\cdot T\neq k\times T$ if $k>1$).
